subtitle: E-mails, formal and informal, and polite questions
words.intro: You can walk up through the glass dome of the Reichstag and look down on the people who run the country, and you can write to them. They’ve got to answer, more or less.
words.more: Auch im Bundestag · also in parliament

grammar[0].subheading: Two frames, formal and informal, and three points in three paragraphs
grammar[0].blocks[0].title: Two frames
grammar[0].blocks[0].note: Never mix them: one du in a formal e-mail stands out.
grammar[0].blocks[1].title: Three points, three paragraphs
grammar[0].blocks[1].text: A message answers a few points. One short paragraph for each, with *Zuerst … · Außerdem … · Zum Schluss …* — nothing gets lost.
grammar[0].blocks[2].title: Words for the practice page
grammar[0].fact: The German federal election gives you two votes: one for a local candidate and one for a party. The second one decides each party’s share of the seats, and a 2023 reform fixed the size of the house at 630.

grammar[1].subheading: A polite question inside, and how to say what you think
grammar[1].blocks[0].title: A polite question inside
grammar[1].blocks[0].note: Remember A2.2: wrapped questions send the verb to the end.
grammar[1].blocks[1].title: Your opinion
grammar[1].blocks[1].note: *Meiner Meinung nach* counts as one word: the verb comes straight after it.
grammar[1].fact: Germans discuss politics at table much more readily than the English do, and it is not considered rude. But *Wen hast du gewählt?* is a real intimacy: your vote is secret, and many long marriages have got by without ever finding out.

practise[2].instruction: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
practise[3].title: Say it in German
practise[4].instruction: Write to your town about your street. Begin and end it properly.
practise[4].note: The middle is your own. Check the verb after meiner Meinung nach and after ob.
listen.intro: Opinions, line by line. Hear each one, say it after the voice, then give it a reason of your own.
speak.intro: The same phrases, in your own mouth: say what you think about something in the news, and why.

document.caption: Ein Stimmzettel: Wie wählt man?
document.intro: The top of a real specimen ballot, for a district election in Saxony in 2025. *Amtlich* means official. These few lines are as official as German gets, and they tell you exactly what to do.
document.fact: A ballot in Germany is printed on paper and counted by hand, in public, in the evening, by volunteers from the neighbourhood. Anyone may stay and watch. It takes a few hours, and it’s very hard to fake.
document.tasks[1].items[2].prompt: Could you tell me when the election is?
reading.intro: There are too few benches on Frau Huber’s street. So she writes to their member of the Bundestag, and Maya types. The member is very polite, and makes one small mistake: she answers.
reading.fact: Anyone may visit the Reichstag dome free of charge, if they register in advance. Norman Foster designed it so the people can stand above the parliament, literally. And citizens can petition the Bundestag: above 50,000 signatures a petition earns a public hearing.
